comparator.name: Literary and Cultural Analysis (Literary Studies)
comparator.sourceNotes: The current official UvA study-programme page reconstructs a complete 180-EC curriculum. Year 1 contains six named compulsory components totalling 60 EC, including close-reading, literary-cultural analysis, narratology, world literature, contemporary arts/media/culture and cultural memory. Year 2 contains four named compulsory components totalling 36 EC, 6 EC of degree-programme restricted choice and 18 EC of free choice. Year 3 contains Philosophy of the Humanities, a thesis workshop and Current Debates at 6 EC each, 6 EC of degree-programme restricted choice, 24 EC of free choice and a 12-EC thesis. The published choice spaces are retained at their stated values without selecting options for UCR convenience.

questions: How is meaning produced through close reading of literature, images, art and popular culture?
How do cultural forms reflect and shape society, identity, inequality and political power?
How do literary and cultural forms travel across media, periods and social contexts?

selection.assessment: The broad closest match owns the general literary-and-cultural-analysis, literary-studies, interpretation, cultural-artefact and literature/philosophy interests. Two further generator-backed directions are coherent, feasible and materially distinct: culture, identity and power; and literature, film and cultural communication. Their schedules differ pairwise by seven to fourteen courses and all satisfy the hard constraints, so the maximum of three alternatives is reached.

alternatives.label: Literary, Artistic & Cultural Analysis
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum integrates literary close reading and theory with art history, film and media, cultural memory, philosophy, sociology and qualitative and historical research.
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response combines literary interpretation and theory with visual art, film, media and cultural history, supported by philosophy, sociology and humanities research.
progression: Introductory art history, literary studies, film and media, history and sociology precede advanced museum studies, media and race, film and text, social theory, cultural communication and independent research. The schedule observes the available semesters and develops foundational interpretive work before advanced research and criticism.

alternatives.label: Culture, Identity & Power
alternatives.labelReason: The curriculum studies culture through history, political thought, sociology, media, literature, heritage and social movements, with sustained attention to inequality, identity and power.
alternatives.concept: A social and political cultural-analysis route organised around identity, colonialism, inequality and power across history, media, literature, art and heritage, supported by political philosophy, sociology and research.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest match, this route replaces most art-history, literary-analysis and creative-communication study with political philosophy, comparative and international politics, empire, gender history, social movements, heritage and conflict. Fourteen of the 24 courses differ, and culture is organised around identity and power rather than broad analysis across artistic media.
progression: Foundations in history, political philosophy, sociology, gender, ethics, comparative politics, media and literature precede advanced social theory, EU politics, media and race, heritage, conflict and historical research. Every course is offered in its assigned semester; there are no unmet formal prerequisites.

alternatives.label: Literature, Film & Cultural Communication
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum forms a clear sequence in literature, film, media, rhetoric and creative communication, complemented by art history, archaeology, philosophy and qualitative research.
alternatives.concept: A text, screen and communication route connecting literary interpretation, film and media analysis, adaptation, rhetoric and creative communication with art history, cultural theory and qualitative research.
alternatives.distinctness: Compared with the closest match, this route removes broad art-history coverage, Renaissance study, sociology, social theory and historical research. It adds rhetoric, material culture, environmental media, philosophy and advanced persuasive communication, with seven courses differing from the closest match and fourteen from the identity-and-power route. The organising emphasis is interpretation and communication across text and screen.
progression: Introductions to literature, media and rhetoric precede advanced film-and-text, media-and-race, literary-meaning, persuasive-communication and creative-communication work. Historical, archaeological, philosophical and qualitative foundations support comparative interpretation. Every course is offered in its assigned semester; there are no unmet formal prerequisites.

blocks: UCR studies art in historical context and changing interpretation, covering a defined visual-arts part of the broader cultural-memory component.
Both engage critically with theories of authorship, interpretation, power and historical disciplinary practice; UCR is art-historiographical rather than broadly literary-cultural.
Both introduce close reading, literary interpretation and foundational concepts for analysing texts and culture.
Both examine how stylistic, rhetorical and visual-form choices produce meaning; UCR concentrates on language and style.
Both introduce critical concepts for analysing contemporary media, images and popular culture.
Both take a comparative global approach to literary traditions and their cultural meanings.
Both mobilise theory through focused cultural case studies; UCR centres race and ethnicity in media.
Both analyse narrative construction across media; UCR focuses specifically on adaptation from text to film.
Both examine relations among culture, media, technology and environmental or material questions.
Both engage advanced contemporary theory and debate; UCR approaches these debates through social theory and civil society.
Both provide philosophical foundations for humanities interpretation; UCR surveys historical philosophical traditions rather than philosophy of the humanities as a field.

notes.text: The UvA programme requires an integrated sequence in poetic and visual analysis, discourse and narratology, literary-cultural theory, cultural memory, critical histories, object-to-case-study research, thesis preparation and a 12-EC thesis. UCR can build strong combinations in literary analysis, film and media, art history, communication, philosophy, sociology, politics and research, but it has fewer dedicated literary-cultural theory and methods components and no compulsory bachelor thesis; the standardised Optional independent research element remains optional.
